title: How Books Got into the Bible
lead: The canon (from Greek kanōn, "measuring rod") is the list of books accepted as Scripture. Jews, Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants agree on most of it, and a few books were debated for centuries.

sections.h: The Hebrew Bible and the extra books
sections.b: The Jewish Bible, the Tanakh, has three parts: the Law (Torah), the Prophets (Nevi'im) and the Writings (Ketuvim). Jesus speaks of what was written "in the Law of Moses, in the Prophets and in the Psalms" (Luke 24:44). The Septuagint, the Greek translation used by many early Christians, also contained books such as Tobit, Judith, Sirach, Wisdom, 1–2 Maccabees and additions to Esther and Daniel. The Catholic Church affirmed these "deuterocanonical" books at the Council of Trent (1546); Protestants call them the Apocrypha and, following Jerome's doubts, keep them out of the Old Testament or print them separately; Orthodox churches accept a somewhat larger set; the Ethiopian Orthodox canon is larger still and includes 1 Enoch and Jubilees. The older theory that a rabbinic "Council of Jamnia" (about AD 90) closed the Jewish canon is now widely doubted.

sections.h: Disputed books of the New Testament
sections.b: By about AD 200 the four Gospels, Acts and Paul's letters were accepted almost everywhere. Some books took longer. Around AD 325 Eusebius listed James, Jude, 2 Peter and 2–3 John among the "disputed" books (antilegomena) that most churches nonetheless used; Hebrews and Revelation were debated too. Athanasius's Easter letter of 367 lists the 27 books of today's New Testament. The original Syriac Bible (the Peshitta) left out 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude and Revelation.
